quizzes.prompt: You see “You don’t have access to GitHub Copilot.” What can you do?

options.text: Use the free option, subscribe to a plan, or join an organization that provides access

options.feedback: The CLI isn’t the problem. Copilot CLI needs an active Copilot subscription.
Signing in won’t help without Copilot access. Get access first.

explain.correct: Right. Copilot CLI needs an active Copilot subscription, and you can check your status at github.com/settings/copilot.
explain.wrong: Copilot CLI needs Copilot access: the free option, a plan, or an organization that provides it.

quizzes.situation: You don’t want to install any of the prerequisites on your computer.

options.text: Fork the repository, then **Code** > **Codespaces** > **Create codespace on main**
Clone the repository and install everything on your own machine
options.feedback: That works too, but then you install the prerequisites yourself. A Codespace has them ready.

options.text: You can’t use the course without installing things locally
options.feedback: You can. A GitHub Codespace has GitHub Copilot CLI ready to go.

explain.correct: Right. A Codespace has GitHub Copilot CLI ready to go, and pre-installs Python and pytest. You’ll just need to sign in.
explain.wrong: A GitHub Codespace is the zero-setup way: fork, then **Code** > **Codespaces** > **Create codespace on main**.

quizzes.prompt: You’ve got Node.js installed. What’s a quick way to get the CLI?

options.feedback: That’s Homebrew, for macOS or Linux. With Node.js, npm is the quick way.
That’s WinGet, for Windows. With Node.js, npm is the quick way.

explain.correct: Right. If you have Node.js installed, npm is a quick way to get the CLI.
explain.wrong: Not sure which to pick? Use `npm` if you have Node.js installed. Otherwise, choose the option that matches your system.

quizzes.situation: You’re signing in to Copilot CLI over SSH, on a server with no browser.
quizzes.prompt: How do you finish signing in?

options.text: Visit github.com/login/device in a browser on another machine, and enter the one-time code
Wait for a browser to open on the server
options.feedback: On a remote or headless terminal, there’s no browser to open. You get a one-time code instead.

options.text: Skip signing in: the CLI works without it
options.feedback: You need to sign in with your GitHub account.

explain.correct: Right. That’s the device code flow: the terminal shows a one-time code, and you enter it at github.com/login/device.
explain.wrong: On a remote or headless terminal, Copilot CLI falls back to the device code flow.

quizzes.situation: You want to send: “Say hello and tell me what you can help with.”

options.text: At Copilot CLI’s prompt (the speaking tube to the crew)
Straight into the shell (the engine-room hatch)
options.feedback: The shell runs commands like `cd` and `ls`. Requests to Copilot go at its prompt, once you’ve started `copilot`.

explain.correct: Yes! Start `copilot`, then ask at its prompt. You should get a friendly response listing what Copilot CLI can help with.
explain.wrong: Requests go to Copilot at its prompt, after you start `copilot`.

quizzes.prompt: Which prompt asks Copilot about the book app’s main file?

options.feedback: Copilot may not know which file you mean. An `@` and the file’s path points it at the file.
That’s a shell command that changes folders. It doesn’t ask Copilot anything.

explain.correct: Right. You should get a summary of the book app’s main functions and commands.
explain.wrong: Point Copilot at the file with `@` and its path.

quizzes.prompt: Put the quick start in order.

items.text: Get the course samples: a Codespace, or a clone
Install Copilot CLI (a Codespace has it already)
Start `copilot` at the repository root and trust the folder
Ask a prompt to check it works

explain.correct: That’s the quick start: the samples, the CLI, the folder, the sign-in, then a test prompt.
explain.wrong: You sign in after you’ve started the CLI and trusted the folder, and you test it once you’re signed in.

quizzes.prompt: Match each way to install Copilot CLI to its command.

explain.correct: Right. Choose what works for your system: npm, Homebrew, WinGet, or the install script.
explain.wrong: Homebrew is `brew`, WinGet is `winget`, the install script comes through `curl`, and npm installs `@github/copilot`.

quizzes.prompt: On a remote or headless terminal, your browser doesn’t open. What then?

options.text: Visit github.com/login/device and enter the one-time code the terminal shows

options.feedback: The install’s fine. Without a browser, you use the device code flow.

options.text: Copy a token from the CLI into the browser
options.feedback: The terminal shows a one-time code, and you enter it at github.com/login/device.

explain.correct: Right. That’s the device code flow.
explain.wrong: Without a browser, Copilot CLI falls back to the device code flow.

quizzes.prompt: Your terminal says “copilot: command not found”. What does that mean?

options.text: The CLI isn’t installed. Try a different installation method

options.feedback: That’s a different message. “command not found” means the CLI isn’t installed.
You can’t run `/login` before the CLI is installed.

explain.correct: Right. If one method failed (say, `brew`), try npm or the install script.
explain.wrong: “command not found” means the CLI isn’t installed.

quizzes.prompt: Which of these mean you’ve got Copilot access at github.com/settings/copilot? Pick all that apply.

options.text: Just a GitHub account, with no Copilot access

explain.correct: Right: Individual, Business, Enterprise, or GitHub Education. Copilot CLI needs an active Copilot subscription.
explain.wrong: A GitHub account alone isn’t enough. Copilot CLI needs an active Copilot subscription.

quizzes.prompt: How often do you sign in to Copilot CLI?

options.text: Once. It persists until your token expires, or you sign out
At the start of every session

options.feedback: The sign-in persists across sessions. You only do it once.

explain.correct: Right. One-time authentication: it persists until your token expires.

quizzes.prompt: The first time you start `copilot` in a folder, what does it ask?

options.text: To trust the folder, one time or across all future sessions

options.feedback: It asks you to trust the folder first. Then you can sign in.
It asks you to trust the folder containing the repository.

explain.correct: Right. You can trust it one time, or across all future sessions.
explain.wrong: It asks you to trust the folder containing the repository.

pages.title: What you need
pages.caption: Two things first. **GitHub Account**: one with Copilot access. **Terminal basics**: you’re comfortable with commands like `cd` and `ls`. Students and teachers can get Copilot Pro free through GitHub Education.

pages.title: What Copilot access means
pages.caption: GitHub Copilot CLI needs an active Copilot subscription. Check your status at [github.com/settings/copilot](https://github.com/settings/copilot): you should see **Copilot Individual**, **Copilot Business**, **Copilot Enterprise**, or **GitHub Education**.

pages.title: A Codespace: zero setup
pages.caption: [Fork the repository](https://github.com/github/copilot-cli-for-beginners/fork), then select **Code** > **Codespaces** > **Create codespace on main**. GitHub Copilot CLI is ready to go (you’ll need to sign in), with Python and pytest pre-installed. To check it, run:

pages.title: Or clone it
pages.caption: To run Copilot CLI on your own machine with the course samples, clone the repository first.

pages.title: Install Copilot CLI
pages.caption: Pick one. Not sure which? Use `npm` if you have Node.js installed. Otherwise, choose the option that matches your system: Homebrew (macOS/Linux), WinGet (Windows), or the install script (macOS/Linux).
pages.code:
npm install -g @github/copilot
brew install copilot-cli
winget install GitHub.Copilot
curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash

pages.title: Trust the folder, then sign in
pages.caption: Start `copilot` at the root of the repository and trust the folder, one time or across all future sessions. Then type `/login` and select **Sign in with your browser (recommended)**. On a remote or headless terminal, you get a one-time code to enter at [github.com/login/device](https://github.com/login/device).

pages.title: Check it works
pages.caption: At Copilot CLI’s prompt, ask this. You should get a friendly response listing Copilot CLI’s capabilities. Demo output varies: your model, tools, and responses will differ. Type `/exit` to leave the CLI.
pages.code: Say hello and tell me what you can help with

pages.title: Try it with the book app
pages.caption: In the shell, `python book_app.py list` (in `samples/book-app-project`) lists five books. Back at the repository root, start `copilot` and ask about the app’s main file. You should get a summary of its main functions and commands.

pages.title: “copilot: command not found”
pages.caption: The CLI isn’t installed. Try a different installation method: if `brew` failed, try `npm install -g @github/copilot`, or the install script.

pages.title: “You don’t have access to GitHub Copilot”
pages.caption: Check you have a Copilot subscription at [github.com/settings/copilot](https://github.com/settings/copilot), and that your organization permits CLI access if you’re using a work account.

pages.title: “Authentication failed”
pages.caption: Sign in again: start `copilot`, then run `/login`. A token that’s expired works the same way: run `/login` again.

pages.title: The browser doesn’t open
pages.caption: On a remote or headless terminal, the device code flow is used instead. Your terminal shows a one-time code: visit [github.com/login/device](https://github.com/login/device), enter it, then authorize access.

glossary.definition: Command Line Interface: a text-based way to work with software, like GitHub Copilot CLI.
A command starting with `/` that controls Copilot, such as `/login` and `/exit`.
A conversation with Copilot that keeps its context and can be resumed later.
